definition: The standard clinical Spanish term for the penis, used in medical, educational, and formal contexts across the entire Spanish-speaking world.
Spanish adaptation of Greek/Latin 'phallus'; used in academic, psychoanalytic, literary, and art-historical discourse as a symbol of male sexuality or power beyond mere anatomy.
notes: Carries heavy symbolic weight in Lacanian psychoanalysis ('el falo' as the master signifier) and in discussions of phallic imagery in art and architecture; this elevates it above pure anatomy.

definition: Lit. 'virile member'; a standard literary and journalistic euphemism for the penis, used when both clinical and crude vocabulary are to be avoided.
notes: The preferred periphrasis in Spanish-language newspapers and literary prose. 'Viril' carries connotations of masculine potency that the purely anatomical 'pene' lacks.

definition: Lit. 'male genital organ'; a clinical descriptive periphrasis used in formal medical, legal, and sex-education texts when maximum decorum is required.
notes: Typically deployed as a noun phrase rather than a lexical item; more common in legal documents, clinical reports, and formal sex-ed materials than in speech.

definition: The glans penis: the cone-shaped distal head of the penis and the most densely innervated part of the external male genitalia.
notes: Masculine noun in Spanish (el glande). Known to most educated adults but rarely used in casual speech; recognition drops among those with minimal formal sex education.

definition: The retractable fold of skin covering the glans penis in uncircumcised males; the foreskin.
notes: Recognition is somewhat lower than other anatomical terms because circumcision is uncommon in Latin America and Spain, making the concept familiar but the clinical term less frequently invoked in practice.

definition: The urethra: the duct carrying urine from the bladder and, in males, semen during ejaculation; the central conduit of the penis.
notes: Applies anatomically to both sexes; listed here because it is the primary internal channel of the male organ. Widely taught in school biology curricula.

definition: Corpus cavernosum: one of the paired columns of erectile tissue in the penis that engorge with blood to produce erection.
notes: Highly specialized anatomical term; recognized mainly by healthcare professionals, medical students, and the well-educated. Below-average recognition reflects the term's absence from standard school curricula.

definition: The dominant crude Spain-Spanish slang for the penis; equivalent in frequency and register to English 'cock'.
notes: Absolutely central to Spanish (Spain) vulgar vocabulary and well-known across Latin America via media. 'Una polla' also means 'a hen' (poultry), which produces constant comic ambiguity. Common in expletives: '¡una polla!', 'me importa una polla'.

definition: The dominant crude Latin American slang for the penis; also one of the most versatile expletive intensifiers in Mexican and Central American Spanish.
notes: Literally 'yardarm' (nautical spar). Extremely productive in fixed expressions: '¡qué verga!' (exclamation of frustration/surprise), 'vale verga' (it's worthless), 'a toda verga' (at full speed). Possibly the highest-frequency vulgar noun in Mexican Spanish.

definition: Crude Spain-Spanish slang for the penis, strongest in Andalusia, Extremadura, and Castile.
notes: Less widespread in Spain's north; used in dismissive phrases like 'en la picha' (in the dick = nowhere, dismissal). Some use also documented in parts of the Southern Cone via migration but primarily Iberian.

definition: Mild, often childlike slang for the penis; literally 'whistle' or 'horn'; used across the entire Spanish-speaking world.
notes: One of the most universally recognized penis slang terms in Spanish, often used with young children or in humorous contexts. Central to the fixed expression 'no me importa un pito' (I couldn't care less), where the trivializing sense of 'whistle' carries the semantic weight.

definition: Crude slang for the penis; literally 'tail'; predominantly used in Spain.
notes: Shares the 'tail' metaphor with several other languages. The idiom 'irse con el rabo entre las piernas' (to leave with one's tail between one's legs) deliberately exploits the double meaning for added humiliation.

definition: Crude slang for the penis; literally 'turnip'; used primarily in Spain as a humorous or mildly derogatory term.
notes: The vegetable homonym makes double entendres unavoidable whenever turnips appear in conversation or on menus. Also used as a mild insult for a stupid person, mirroring English 'dick' used as an insult.

definition: Crude regional slang for the penis; used in southern and central Spain and independently in Central America (Honduras, Nicaragua).
notes: In Spain also means 'stupid person' or 'idiot' as a secondary meaning. In Central America the sexual meaning is primary. Etymology is disputed — possibly from Basque or Arabic substrate. Its dual distribution across Spain and Central America reflects independent parallel development.

definition: Extremely crude River Plate (Argentina/Uruguay) slang for the penis; among the most vulgar penis terms in Rioplatense Spanish.
notes: So strongly associated with the River Plate that other Spanish speakers immediately tag it as Argentinian or Uruguayan. 'Una poronga' used as a dismissal means 'absolutely nothing'. Widely known outside the region through Argentine film and television.

definition: Very crude River Plate (Argentina/Uruguay) slang for the penis; also used as a general expletive and intensifier.
notes: Uniquely in Argentine Spanish, 'pija' has a second entirely unrelated meaning: 'posh' or 'preppy' (describing upper-class affectation). This creates sharp contextual ambiguity and frequent humor specific to Rioplatense. The duality is not present in Uruguayan usage.

definition: Very crude slang for the penis; dominant in Caribbean Spanish (Cuba, Venezuela, Dominican Republic, Colombia) and widely understood across Latin America.
notes: Highly productive in fixed expressions: 'no me importa una pinga', 'esto es una pinga' (this is terrible/worthless). Despite phonetic similarity to 'picha', the two terms developed independently and carry distinct regional distributions.

definition: Very crude Chilean slang for the penis; also used as a general expletive and dismissive intensifier in Chilean Spanish.
notes: Strongly Chilean and largely unknown outside Chile. Produces a sharp semantic collision with the Quechua/Andean Spanish word 'minga' (communal labor), which is entirely unrelated and carries respectful connotations in Andean communities.

definition: Crude Mexican slang for the penis; in the same dialect also slang for the police, derived from Caló.
notes: The double meaning (penis/police) creates significant contextual ambiguity in Mexican street speech; the police meaning comes from Romani-influenced Caló. Predominantly Mexico and Central America; less common in South America or Spain.

definition: Crude slang for the penis; literally 'bar', 'beam', or 'heavy bolt used to barricade a door'; the metaphor emphasizes size and rigidity.
notes: The literal meaning (a thick wooden bar) makes the metaphor self-evident and size-emphasizing. Used in Spain and various Latin American countries. Also used in 'agarrar una tranca' meaning to get very drunk, illustrating how the word operates in multiple unrelated idiomatic domains.

definition: Slang for the penis; literally 'bug', 'insect', or 'small creature'; used primarily in Spain.
notes: The primary meaning (insect/creature/animal) dominates across Latin America, where the sexual meaning is weak or absent. In Puerto Rico, 'bicho' refers to the vagina rather than the penis, demonstrating a complete regional semantic inversion. Recognition score reflects Spain-primary usage of the sexual meaning.

definition: Mild euphemistic slang for the penis; literally 'dove' or 'pigeon'; primarily used in Mexico and Central America, often in speech directed at children.
notes: Considered childlike and unthreatening; the dove metaphor appears across Romance-language traditions. In Mexico also used in the expression 'sacar la paloma' (to take out the dove = to expose the penis). Recognized broadly because the term 'paloma' is ubiquitous, but the sexual meaning is strongest in the Mexican register.

definition: Crude slang for the penis; literally 'club', 'cudgel', or 'garrote'; the metaphor emphasizes blunt size and force.
notes: The primary meanings (a heavy wooden stick and Spain's traditional method of capital punishment by strangulation) give the metaphor both a size implication and an inadvertently sinister connotation. Less frequent than 'polla' but widely understood in Spain.

definition: Mild diminutive slang for the penis; the '-ín' suffix (of Asturian-Leonese origin) imparts a childlike or affectionate tone; used primarily in northern and central Spain.
notes: The diminutive register makes this functionally equivalent to English 'willy' or 'winkle' — inoffensive enough for parental use. Often deployed humorously by adults to deflate sexual tension. The '-ín' suffix is a northern Iberian diminutive variant, distinguishing this from the more widespread '-ito' form.

definition: Crude slang for the penis, dominant in Chilean vernacular and common across Peru, Bolivia, and parts of Central America.
notes: The default crude penis word in Chile; also used in Peru and Bolivia; less common in Mexico and largely unknown in Spain.

definition: Rioplatense slang for the penis.
notes: Primarily Argentina and Uruguay; 'Pirulo' is also the brand name of a popular ice cream bar in the region, generating persistent double entendres.

definition: Iberian Spanish slang for the penis, derived from the black poplar tree (chopo), whose tall, columnar form evokes a phallus.
notes: Primarily Spain; the black poplar is known for its straight, upright growth habit; limited penetration in Latin America.

definition: Slang for the penis using the word for 'log' or 'trunk,' implying substantial size and rigidity.
notes: Used across Spain and Latin America; implies a thick or large member; 'tronco' also means 'mate/buddy' in colloquial Spanish, occasionally producing ambiguity.

definition: Slang for the penis derived from 'mallet' or 'sledgehammer,' emphasizing forceful size.
notes: Primarily Iberian Spanish; the mallet metaphor foregrounds force and heft rather than length; less common than tronco across Latin America.

definition: Euphemistic slang for the penis using the word for 'walking stick' or 'cane,' playing on upright phallic shape.
notes: A mild, humorous metaphor used across Spanish-speaking regions; lower vulgarity than direct penis slang.

definition: English loanword adopted into Spanish as humorous slang for the penis, referencing the handheld video-game controller.
notes: Peak usage late 1990s–early 2000s, aligned with the rise of home gaming; still recognized but less actively used; same metaphor exists in English.

definition: Euphemistic slang for the penis using the word for 'cucumber,' a widespread vegetable-shape metaphor.
notes: One of the most widespread penis euphemisms in Spanish; the cucumber metaphor appears across many languages; 'no importar un pepino' (not to care a cucumber) adds ironic layering in Spain.

definition: Euphemistic slang for the penis using the word for 'carrot,' referencing its elongated tapered shape.
notes: More playful than crude; less common than pepino as a penis metaphor in Spanish; the carrot's color and taper evoke the circumcised glans.

definition: Slang for the penis using the word for 'bone,' playing on both structural hardness and the English cognate 'boner' for erection.
notes: The bone-erection metaphor works cross-linguistically; can specifically connote erection rather than the flaccid organ; used across Latin America and Spain.

definition: Euphemistic slang for the penis using the word for 'tool,' one of the most universal phallic metaphors across human languages.
notes: Maps directly to the English slang 'tool'; among the mildest and most socially acceptable penis euphemisms in Spanish; widely used in humorous contexts.

definition: Mild euphemism for the penis using the word for 'apparatus' or 'device,' used in quasi-clinical and humorous registers.
notes: One of the most demure penis references in Spanish; also appears in clinical contexts as 'aparato reproductor' (reproductive system), lending it a veneer of respectability even in crude usage.

definition: Mexican slang for the penis derived from 'pirinola,' a traditional wooden spinning top with a tapered, pointed tip.
notes: Primarily Mexican Spanish; the pirinola's pointed spinning tip and the act of spinning map onto penetrative connotations; limited recognition outside Mexico.

definition: Crude slang for the penis, literally 'beak' or 'tip'; among the most taboo penis terms in Chile, approaching the vulgarity ceiling of Chilean profanity.
notes: In Chile, 'pico' rivals 'pichula' in vulgarity and is censored on broadcast television; also used in Colombia and Peru; 'al pico' functions as a strong dismissive expletive in Chilean Spanish.

definition: Mexican and Central American slang for the penis, sometimes carrying connotations of thickness or large size.
notes: Primarily Mexico and Central America; in non-sexual registers 'choncho' can mean 'fat' or 'chubby,' which transfers into the size implication in sexual use.

definition: Rioplatense slang for the penis; literally 'Turk,' likely originating from ethnic stereotypes about Levantine immigrants in Argentina.
notes: Primarily Argentina; Argentina received substantial Levantine Arab immigration in the 19th–20th centuries, colloquially called 'turcos'; the ethnic attribution of sexual prowess to this group appears to underlie the slang.

definition: Rioplatense slang for the penis; literally a squat clay jug or earthenware pot, metaphorically referencing genital shape.
notes: Primarily Argentina and Uruguay; in Uruguay 'botija' separately means 'kid' or 'boy' in everyday slang, adding double-meaning potential; low recognition outside the River Plate region.

definition: Augmentative of 'polla' (the dominant Iberian Spanish crude term for penis), meaning a large penis; the '-ón' suffix marks exceptional size.
notes: Derived from 'polla' + augmentative '-ón'; primarily Iberian Spanish where 'polla' is the default vulgar penis word; register and tone parallel English 'big dick.'

definition: Spanish slang for the glans penis; literally 'cocoon' or 'flower bud,' evoking the rounded tip of the penis; simultaneously a high-frequency general insult in Spain.
notes: Has dual currency in Spain: anatomically specific (glans) and as a general-purpose insult roughly equivalent to British 'bellend' or 'knob'; both meanings are simultaneously active; less common in Latin America.

definition: The clinical term for the internal muscular canal extending from the cervix to the vulvar vestibule; the standard anatomical term in Spanish medical and educational contexts.
notes: Identical spelling to the English clinical term; Latin origin; frequently misapplied by lay speakers to denote the external genitalia (vulva) as well.

definition: The clinical term for the external female genitalia, encompassing the labia majora and minora, clitoris, and vaginal opening.
notes: Identical to the English clinical term; significantly underrecognized by the general population relative to 'vagina,' despite being the visible external anatomy; recognition has risen with sex-education campaigns.

definition: The clinical Spanish term for the vaginal lips (labia), used generically to cover both the labia majora and labia minora.
notes: Generic clinical term; the more precise distinction is 'labios mayores' (labia majora) and 'labios menores' (labia minora); 'labios vaginales' is preferred in sex-education contexts for accessibility.

definition: The clinical Spanish term for the vaginal introitus — the external entrance to the vaginal canal.
notes: Highly specialized medical terminology; rarely encountered outside gynecological or anatomical discourse; the full form 'introito vaginal' is more common in clinical writing than the standalone noun.

definition: The clinical and literary Spanish term for the mons pubis — the rounded fatty prominence over the pubic symphysis; literally 'Mount of Venus.'
notes: Translates Latin 'mons Veneris'; bridges clinical anatomy and literary tradition via the mythological reference to Venus; known to educated speakers but not universally recognized.

definition: The clinical Spanish term specifically denoting the internal muscular channel of the vagina from the cervix to the vaginal opening.
notes: More anatomically precise than 'vagina' alone, emphasizing the tubular structure; common in obstetric contexts (e.g., 'parto por canal vaginal' = vaginal delivery).

definition: The most widespread and forceful crude Spanish slang for the vagina; also functions as a standalone expletive analogous to English 'fuck' or 'shit'.
notes: In Spain the expletive use (¡coño!) is so pervasive that the anatomical force is often weakened; in Latin America the anatomical reference remains more foregrounded and carries stronger shock value.

definition: Crude Spanish slang for the vagina, primarily used in Spain.
notes: In Spain 'chocho' also informally means a sentimental or doting person (from 'chochear,' to become senile with affection); the sexual meaning predominates in sexual contexts but the dual use is common.

definition: Highly offensive Rioplatense slang for the vagina; in all other Spanish dialects the word innocuously means 'shell' (seashell, mollusc shell).
notes: The sexual meaning is essentially exclusive to Argentina and Uruguay; everywhere else 'concha' is a neutral everyday word. This creates persistent miscommunication and dark comedy when Rioplatense speakers use the word abroad.

definition: Crude slang for the vagina literally meaning 'crack,' 'split,' or 'slit,' used across the Spanish-speaking world.
notes: The dual meaning (crack/split in general usage; vagina in sexual slang) is context-dependent and understood pan-regionally. One of the more anatomically descriptive metaphors in this list.

definition: Dialectal Spanish slang for the vagina, primarily used in eastern and southern Spain (Valencia, Catalonia, Aragon regions).
notes: A relatively regional term with limited penetration outside Spain. May derive from a crevice-related etymological root. Low recognition in Latin America.

definition: In Cuba and parts of the Caribbean, slang for the vagina derived from the tropical fruit of the same name; elsewhere in the Spanish-speaking world the word refers only to the fruit.
notes: The sexual meaning is so dominant in Cuba that Cubans typically substitute 'fruta bomba' when referring to the papaya fruit to avoid the double entendre. In Mexico, Spain, and most of Latin America the word is entirely innocent.

definition: Mexican crude slang for the vagina; the word also refers to a type of unrefined brown-sugar sweet or a bundle of dried grain husks in non-sexual contexts.
notes: The innocent meanings (brown-sugar candy, cornhusk bundle) coexist with the crude slang in Mexico, producing constant double entendres. Also used in parts of Central America in the sexual sense.

definition: Crude slang for the vagina used primarily in Venezuela, Colombia, and parts of the Caribbean.
notes: Also used informally in some Venezuelan and Colombian families as a children's word for the vagina, which reduces its shock value relative to other terms. Augmentative 'totona' is also attested.

definition: Crude Spanish slang for the vagina; the standard meaning of the word is a soft bread roll or bun.
notes: The baked-goods metaphor is widespread in Spain; the sexual meaning also exists in Cuba and parts of Latin America. The dual use generates food-related double entendres in Spanish speech.

definition: Crude Andalusian and southern Spanish slang for the vagina, with limited distribution outside that region.
notes: Primarily a term from Andalusia and Extremadura in southern Spain. Virtually unknown in Latin America. Etymology uncertain.

definition: Slang for the vagina derived from the word for clam, referencing the bivalve's shape; used across Spain and much of Latin America.
notes: The food metaphor (clam/bivalve) gives this slightly softer connotations than terms like 'coño,' though it is still distinctly crude. Widely understood pan-regionally.

definition: Caribbean and Central American slang for the vagina; in Mexico the same word (typically plural 'chichis') primarily refers to breasts instead.
notes: Significant regional semantic divergence: Mexican 'chichis' = breasts; Cuban and Central American 'chichi' = vagina. Derived from babytalk reduplication. Moderate crude score reflects the infantilizing diminutive form.

definition: A pan-regional Spanish euphemism for the vagina meaning 'cave,' understood across the Spanish-speaking world.
notes: The cave metaphor is transparent and widely understood; its euphemistic register makes it substantially less offensive than direct anatomical slang. Appears frequently in ribald humor and double-entendre wordplay.

definition: Cuban and Central American slang for the vagina; in other Spanish dialects the word refers to a tobacco pipe or, in some regions, a well or water source.
notes: The innocent meanings (tobacco pipe, water source) coexist with the sexual slang in different regions. The sexual meaning is primary in Cuba and parts of Central America. Also used in some Colombian dialects.

definition: A mild Spanish slang term for the vagina derived from 'minino' (a small cat or kitten), directly parallel to English 'pussy' in its kitten-derived etymology.
notes: The closest structural equivalent to English 'pussy' in Spanish — same animal, same metaphorical extension, similar register. Mild enough to appear in mainstream Spanish media. More common in Spain than Latin America.

definition: A widespread crude slang term for the vagina used across Spain and Latin America.
notes: Also a common Spanish nickname (short for various names). In some Colombian and Venezuelan regions 'cuca' refers to a type of insect or beetle. The sexual meaning is well-established across most dialects.

definition: Colombian crude slang for the vagina; in standard Spanish the word means the seed, pit, or stone of a fruit.
notes: The sexual meaning is specific to Colombia and nearby Andean regions; elsewhere 'pepa' simply means a fruit seed or, in some Latin American drug slang, a pill. Also a nickname for women named Josefa.

definition: Crude slang for the vagina distributed across Spain and Latin America; a feminine-form variant related to the Iberian Spanish term 'chocho.'
notes: More broadly distributed than 'chocho,' which skews Iberian. In some contexts 'chocha' also serves as an archaic adjective meaning 'senile' or 'doting' (same root as 'chochear'). Also the name of the Eurasian woodcock bird (Scolopax rusticola).

definition: A Spanish euphemistic slang for the vagina derived from 'cotorra' (a small parrot or parakeet), primarily used in Spain.
notes: The sexual meaning is substantially less common than the bird meaning; the word's primary everyday sense is a noisy or chatty person. The vaginal usage is largely Spanish-peninsula-specific with low recognition in Latin America.

definition: A euphemistic literary slang for the vagina meaning 'grotto' or 'cave,' used informally and in sexual humor across the Spanish-speaking world.
notes: One of the softest terms in this list; the primary meaning (natural cave or ornamental garden grotto) vastly predominates. The sexual connotation surfaces mainly in ribald wordplay and erotica rather than casual everyday slang.

definition: A very mild euphemism for the vagina meaning 'little thing,' used pan-regionally in child-directed speech and in adult contexts requiring coy indirection.
notes: Standard in childrearing across the Spanish-speaking world to name genitalia without explicit language. Among adults signals deliberate coyness or embarrassment. The diminutive suffix '-ita' is doing significant register-softening work.

definition: Dominican Republic and broader Caribbean slang for the vagina, derived from the word for sponge cake or biscuit.
notes: The pastry double entendre is characteristic of Caribbean Spanish ribald humor. Also used in Puerto Rico with the same sexual meaning. In Spain and most of Latin America 'bizcocho' refers only to the baked good.

definition: A Chilean compound expletive literally meaning 'your mother's cunt,' functioning as a general-purpose intensifier and insult of maximum severity; the most powerful swearword in Chilean Spanish.
notes: Etymologically derived from the vagina slang 'concha' (Rioplatense/Chilean) combined with 'su madre' (your mother), but the compound functions as a general expletive analogous to English 'motherfucker' rather than as an anatomical reference. Also written 'conchetumadre' in informal orthography. Recognized pan-regionally through Chilean cultural reach.

definition: A low-frequency dialectal Spanish slang term for the vagina with very limited regional distribution.
notes: Among the rarest terms in this list; appears in limited Spanish regional dialects and has minimal documentation. May be hyperlocal or generational. Low inter-regional recognition even within Spain.

definition: Venezuelan and Caribbean slang for the vagina; in standard Spanish the word 'bobo/boba' is the common adjective meaning 'silly,' 'dumb,' or 'foolish.'
notes: The sexual meaning is strongly regional (Venezuela, parts of the Caribbean coast); Spanish speakers outside that region typically know the word only as the adjective meaning 'stupid' or 'silly,' creating potential for confusion or double entendre.

definition: Slang term for the vagina used primarily in Venezuelan and some Colombian Spanish.
notes: Predominantly Caribbean/northern South American usage; rare in Spain or the Southern Cone.

definition: Poetic euphemism for the vagina using the word for 'flower' to evoke femininity and delicacy.
notes: Used in romantic, literary, or coy registers; not clinical but not crude. The English 'flower' is deployed as an identical euphemism.

definition: Childish diminutive euphemism for the vagina used in baby talk or to soften the anatomical reference.
notes: The '-ita' diminutive softens it considerably; primarily deployed when speaking to or about young children regarding anatomy. Geographic distribution is uneven.

definition: Standard formal and semi-clinical Spanish term for the female breasts.
notes: Default elevated-register word; used in medical, journalistic, and polite social contexts. Less technical than 'glándulas mamarias' but more formal than 'pechos'.

definition: Formal term for breasts, cognate with English 'mammary'; used in medical and anatomical contexts.
notes: 'Mamas' also means 'mothers/mamas,' requiring context to disambiguate the anatomical sense.

definition: Fully clinical anatomical term for the mammary glands, used in medical and scientific contexts.
notes: Strictly technical; effectively never used in everyday speech. Direct cognate with English 'mammary glands'.

definition: The pigmented circular area of skin surrounding the nipple; the same term in Spanish and English.
notes: International anatomical term identical in form and meaning to the English. Recognized mainly by those with some medical or sex-education exposure.

definition: The most widely used crude slang term for female breasts across the entire Spanish-speaking world.
notes: Universal across all Spanish dialects; the default vulgar word for breasts. Cognate with Italian 'tette' and Portuguese 'tetas'; etymology from Latin 'tetta'.

definition: Common mild-register term for female breasts, literally 'chests'; acceptable in most social contexts.
notes: Occupies the middle ground between clinical ('senos') and crude ('tetas'); used freely in mainstream media and advertising without being vulgar. Anatomically sex-neutral but culturally applied primarily to female breasts.

definition: Cute, childish slang for breasts, predominantly used in Mexican Spanish.
notes: Strong association with Mexican vernacular; the register mirrors English 'boobies' almost exactly. Familiar to non-Mexican speakers through media but not natively used outside Mexico.

definition: Slang term for breasts common in Mexican and Central American Spanish, slightly more crude than 'bubis'.
notes: Very common in Mexican vernacular and Central America; recognized but not natively used in Spain or South America. Possibly reduplicative baby-talk origin.

definition: Colloquial slang for breasts used in Colombian and some other South American varieties of Spanish.
notes: Named after the common given name Lola; the playful personification via a woman's name is a recurring pattern in Spanish breast slang. Limited geographic spread.

definition: Crude slang for large female breasts, comparing them to melons; implies impressive size.
notes: The English 'melons' and Spanish 'melones' are cognate slang with identical meaning, connotations, and implied size praise; understood across all dialects.

definition: Very crude slang for breasts borrowed from the word for animal udders; derogatory and dehumanizing.
notes: One of the most demeaning terms for breasts in Spanish, directly comparing a woman's body to livestock anatomy. English 'udders' carries the identical dehumanizing charge.

definition: Slang for female breasts used in parts of Spain and Latin America; etymology likely from the feminine given name Dominga.
notes: Personification via a woman's given name follows a common Spanish pattern (cf. 'lolas', 'nenas'). Moderately crude; not universal across all regions.

definition: Humorous-crude slang for female breasts derived from 'chicken breast'; implies fleshy volume.
notes: Primary meaning is the cut of poultry meat; its application to human breasts is comedic and mildly crude. The humor comes from the shared shape and texture association.

definition: Diminutive of 'tetas'; refers to small breasts or is used affectionately to reduce the bluntness of the base term.
notes: The '-itas' diminutive softens 'tetas' slightly but it remains crude. Can imply small size or serve as an affectionate register shift; mirrors English 'titties' closely.

definition: Poetic-humorous euphemism for small, perky breasts; literally 'little doves' or 'popcorn'.
notes: The image is of small, rounded, uplifted forms — either doves or popcorn kernels. Playful and non-offensive; less widely distributed than mainstream slang terms.

definition: Playful slang for breasts using the word for 'little girls/babies'; personifies them as a pair.
notes: Mirrors the English euphemism 'the girls' for breasts — personifying them as a pair of feminine companions. Regional spread uneven; more common in informal online contexts.

definition: Regional slang for female breasts in some Latin American varieties of Spanish.
notes: The primary meaning of 'chola' is an Andean indigenous or mestiza woman (Andean Spanish) or a Chicana gang-affiliated woman (US/MX Spanish), both carrying strong ethnic identity weight; use as breast slang is geographically restricted and risks conflation with those ethnic terms.

definition: Crude slang for breasts using the word for 'balls/spheres'; less common in this sense than its primary use for testicles.
notes: 'Pelotas' primarily means testicles across most dialects (Argentina, Spain); its application to breasts is context-dependent and requires speaker-gender and conversational framing to disambiguate. Listed under breasts per section context.

definition: The standard clinical and formal term for the testicles in Spanish.
notes: Direct cognate with English 'testicles'; used in medical, educational, and formal journalistic contexts. Not inherently vulgar but sounds clinical and stiff in casual speech.

definition: Clinical anatomical term for the gonads (testicles or ovaries), used exclusively in medical and scientific contexts.
notes: Direct cognate with English 'gonads'; sex-neutral term referring to either male or female reproductive glands. Essentially never used in casual speech.

definition: The clinical and anatomical term for the scrotum, the skin pouch enclosing the testicles.
notes: Direct cognate with English 'scrotum'; used in medical contexts. More widely recognized than 'gónadas' due to sex-education exposure but still uncommon in casual speech.

definition: Extremely widespread crude slang for testicles, literally 'eggs'; also used metaphorically for courage or audacity.
notes: One of the most universal Spanish slang terms, understood across all dialects. Primary literal meaning is 'eggs' (food), creating perpetual double-entendre potential; metaphorical extension to courage mirrors English 'balls' precisely.

definition: Very common crude slang for testicles; also widely used metaphorically to mean courage or audacity.
notes: Borrowed into English as a mild intensifier meaning nerve or guts; one of the most internationally recognized Spanish words.

definition: Common slang for testicles; literally 'balls' as in sports balls; also used to mean nerve or audacity.
notes: En pelotas also means 'stark naked.'

definition: Slang for testicles; literally 'balls'; widely used across multiple Spanish-speaking regions.
Crude Mexican slang for testicles; emphatic orthographic variant of huevos (eggs); signals maximally vulgar register.
notes: The gu- spelling instead of standard h- marks intentionally crude emphasis; standard huevos is polysemous enough to be ambiguous out of context.

definition: Regional Iberian Spanish slang for testicles; also the dialectal word for truffles (the fungus) in some areas.
notes: The truffle meaning creates a food-based double entendre; declining in use among younger speakers in Spain.

definition: Mexican slang for testicles, derived from the Nahuatl word tanatli; also used colloquially to mean personal belongings or stuff.
notes: Nahuatl etymology distinguishes this from purely Spanish slang; the dual meaning (testicles and belongings) is common in Mexican colloquial speech.

definition: Humorous crude slang for testicles; literally 'meatballs,' evoking shape similarity.
notes: Primarily Iberian Spanish; relies on meatball shape for humor; less aggressive in tone than cojones.

definition: Playful, somewhat old-fashioned euphemism for testicles used in Spain; not aggressive in register.
notes: Considered quaint or humorous rather than transgressive; less commonly used by younger Spanish speakers; no clear etymology.

definition: Slang for testicles; literally 'coconuts,' evoking shape and paired nature; mildly crude.
notes: Primary meanings of cocos are coconuts and colloquially heads; testicular meaning requires context.

definition: Slang for testicles; literally 'walnuts' or 'nuts'; food metaphor parallel to English 'nuts.'
notes: Shares the same food-to-anatomy metaphorical path as English 'nuts'; not the primary meaning of the word.

definition: Gay; a person, especially a man, sexually attracted to people of the same sex; the dominant everyday term across all Spanish-speaking regions.

definition: Transgender; a person whose gender identity differs from the sex assigned at birth; the contemporary preferred term in Spanish medical, legal, and activist discourse.

definition: Literally 'group sex'; a neutral descriptive phrase for sexual activity involving multiple participants simultaneously.
notes: More clinical and journalistic in tone than 'orgía', which carries stronger transgressive or hedonistic connotations; 'sexo en grupo' is preferred in public health communication, news reporting, and app interfaces.

notes: Used in Spanish exactly as in English — a French loan in both cases. Carries a slightly more romantic or sophisticated register than 'trío', implying possible domestic continuity. More common in educated urban registers and literary/journalistic use.

english_term: a thing (as in 'we have a thing')
notes: 'Tener un rollo con alguien' = to have a thing with someone. Primarily Iberian; in Latin America 'rollo' typically means trouble or a tedious speech, not a relationship.

notes: Primarily Iberian Spanish; related to the verb 'ligar'. Recognition declining among younger Spaniards who adopt English-derived terms.

notes: Primarily Iberian Spanish; Latin American equivalents include 'levantar' or 'conquistar'. Slightly declining among younger speakers in favor of 'pillar'.

notes: Primarily Iberian Spanish; well understood via media exposure but rarely used in this sense in Latin America. Etymology possibly alludes to heat and friction.

notes: 'Echar' functions as a light auxiliary ('to give/throw'). The most characteristic crude sex idiom of Spain; roughly equivalent in crudeness to British 'shag'.

definition: Literally 'to be feeling like it / in the mood'; a mild euphemism for experiencing sexual desire or arousal.
english_term: to be in the mood, to be horny

english_term: to warm up, to get someone going

definition: Diminutive 'the little thing'; an affectionate or childlike euphemism for the genitals, most often the vagina or penis depending on context.

notes: The most minimal possible sexual euphemism; depends entirely on shared context. Pan-Hispanic and timeless.

definition: Literally 'the thing'; a generic euphemism for the genitals or for sex itself without further specification.

definition: Archaic-literary phrase meaning 'carnal matters'; refers to sexual affairs or desires, typically in a moral, religious, or elevated register.
english_term: carnal matters, matters of the flesh
notes: Carries theological weight; more common in older literature, Church contexts, and period drama than in contemporary speech.

definition: Literary phrase meaning 'pleasures of the flesh'; refers broadly to sexual and sensual gratification.
notes: Used in religious, philosophical, and literary registers; evokes the theological tension between spiritual life and physical desire. Pan-Hispanic.

definition: Idiom literally 'between the sheets'; refers to sexual activity or one's conduct and prowess in bed.
notes: Calque of the English idiom; used adverbially ('lo que pasa entre las sábanas') or as a locative euphemism for sexual activity. Pan-Hispanic.

definition: Idiom literally 'to get to the grain / to get to the point'; in sexual context means to skip foreplay and move directly to penetrative sex.
english_term: to get to it, to skip to the main event
notes: Primarily a communication idiom ('cut to the chase'); sexual sense is colloquial and depends on context. Pan-Hispanic.

definition: Verb meaning to make out; to kiss passionately and at length, typically involving tongues and often in a semi-public setting.
notes: Derived from 'morro' (snout/lips in colloquial Castilian). Primarily Iberian; equivalent to 'comerse a besos' or 'besuquearse' in Latin America.

definition: Noun: a makeout session; a sustained exchange of passionate kissing.
notes: Noun derived directly from 'morrear'; same etymology, register, and geographic distribution. Iberian Spanish only.

definition: Idiom literally 'to throw oneself into the envelope/bag'; primarily means to go to bed or nap, but used euphemistically to imply sexual activity in bed.
notes: 'Sobre' refers colloquially to the bed as a container. The sleep meaning is primary; sexual connotation is secondary and highly contextual. Primarily Iberian and declining.

definition: Slang verb meaning to pull or score; to successfully attract and have sex with someone, framed as catching or snagging a conquest.
notes: Primary meaning is 'to catch/grab'; sexual sense is specifically Iberian youth slang. 'Pillar cacho' is a cruder variant meaning to get a piece. Gaining on 'ligar' among younger speakers.

definition: Idiom meaning to have a secret romantic or sexual affair; 'lío' literally means 'mess' or 'tangle,' euphemistically implying an entangled romantic or sexual involvement.
notes: 'Lío' alone can also denote the affair partner or a casual fling; the phrase is deliberately vague enough to cover both emotional and purely sexual entanglements.

definition: Colloquial peninsular-Spanish noun for a sexual romp or fuck, etymologically derived from 'follar'; primary meaning is 'mess' or 'commotion,' and the sexual sense is secondary but well-established in Spain.
notes: Primary sense (mess, ruckus) is pan-Hispanic; the sexual double meaning exploiting the 'follar' root is predominantly Peninsular. Often used for innuendo without committed sexual intent.

definition: Euphemistic phrase meaning 'bedroom matter' or 'bedroom affair,' used to refer obliquely to sexual activity or an ongoing sexual relationship between two people.
notes: Deliberately vague construction; can describe a one-time encounter or a sustained clandestine relationship depending on context. Tactful enough for use in mixed or formal company.

definition: Archaic legal and ecclesiastical term meaning 'carnal union' or 'carnal joining,' denoting sexual intercourse especially in the context of marriage law and annulment proceedings.
notes: 'Ayuntamiento' ordinarily means 'town hall' or 'joining/assembly'; the legal-ecclesiastical phrase was standard in Inquisition records, marriage annulment cases, and theological treatises through the 19th century.

definition: Archaic clinical and legal phrase for 'carnal copulation,' used in ecclesiastical, juridical, and medical texts to denote sexual intercourse with full anatomical detachment.
notes: Frequent in Inquisition trial records, canon law, and 19th-century medical and forensic treatises. The Latin root 'copula' keeps the register clinical; 'carnal' specifies the physical, non-spiritual dimension.

definition: Clinical and legal term for living together as a sexual or romantic couple outside of formal marriage.
notes: Feels bureaucratic or legalistic to most speakers; everyday Spanish prefers 'vivir juntos' or 'pareja de hecho.' Appears in census forms, legal codes, and notarial documents rather than casual speech.

definition: One of the seven deadly sins in Catholic moral theology; intense and unrestrained sexual desire or appetite.
notes: Highly recognizable across all Spanish-speaking cultures due to biblical and catechetical transmission. Carries heavy Catholic moral freight; 'lujurioso/a' is the adjectival form. Used in literary and moral contexts more than in crude slang.

definition: Wanton sexual desire or lascivious conduct; the quality of being sexually immodest, licentious, or given to overt sensual indulgence.
notes: Semantically adjacent to 'lujuria' but emphasizes external behavior and display over interior desire. Common in moral treatises, Inquisition proceedings, and Golden Age drama. Adjectival form: 'lascivo/a.'

definition: Archaic noun denoting sexual immodesty, unchastity, or shameless behavior; the absence of sexual modesty or 'pudor,' especially in conduct.
notes: Directly from Latin 'impudicitia.' Common in patristic texts, moral theology, and Spanish treatises through the 18th century; largely extinct in modern usage. Distinct from 'lujuria' (desire) and 'lascivia' (display) in stressing the absence of shame.

definition: The social and moral dishonor accruing to a woman and her family through sexual transgression — rape, seduction, premarital sex, or adultery — within the Iberian honor-shame system.
notes: Central concept of Golden Age drama (the 'dramas de honor' of Calderón, Lope de Vega). English 'dishonor' lacks the gendered, familial, and sexually specific dimension; 'ruined woman' is approximate but individual rather than systemic. The concept encodes a collective family shame triggered by one woman's sexual status, with no tidy English equivalent.

definition: A woman who cohabits with and is sexually available to a man of higher status without being his legal wife; a concubine.
notes: Widely recognized from biblical transmission and historical literature. Modern usage is almost exclusively historical, literary, or journalistic (historical reportage). The institution was legally regulated in medieval Iberian law.

definition: Archaic term for a mistress, kept woman, or lower-status concubine; a woman maintained by a man outside of marriage for sexual purposes.
notes: 'Mancebo/manceba' originally meant simply 'young man/woman' (from Arabic 'mancab'); the female form acquired sexual connotations of availability. Appears in medieval legal codes and Golden Age literature including Cervantes. Largely extinct; modern readers may not parse the sexual meaning without context.

definition: A woman who lived with a man in 'barraganía,' a semi-legal informal union recognized in medieval Castilian and Aragonese law that granted her certain protections without the full legal status of wife.
notes: Distinct from generic concubinage: 'barraganía' was a legally codified Iberian institution with specific rights (inheritance claims in some fueros). Etymologically from Arabic 'barragan.' Specialists-only term today; virtually no recognition outside medieval history contexts.

definition: To fornicate; to engage in sexual intercourse outside of marriage, framed through a lens of religious and moral condemnation.
notes: Widely recognized from biblical and ecclesiastical transmission; occasionally deployed humorously in modern speech precisely because of its portentous register. The noun form is 'fornicación'; the agent noun 'fornicador/a' is also current.

definition: Carnal sin; in Catholic moral theology, any sexual act considered sinful — primarily fornication, adultery, sodomy, or onanism — framed as an offense against God and nature.
notes: Broader than 'fornication' alone: encompasses all sexual sins in Catholic taxonomy. Appeared ubiquitously in confessional manuals, penitentials, and homiletical literature throughout the Spanish-speaking world. Still recognized in cultures with strong Catholic formation.

definition: Carnal act; an archaic legal, medical, and ecclesiastical euphemism for sexual intercourse, emphasizing the physical dimension over the emotional or moral.
notes: Standard phrasing in Inquisition records, colonial penal codes, and 19th-century forensic medicine. Still surfaces in some Latin American legal contexts. More distancing and clinical than emotionally charged.

definition: Defloration; the act of taking a woman's virginity through first penetrative intercourse, framed around rupture of the hymen.
notes: Botanical metaphor (stripping petals from a flower). Variant form 'desfloración' also circulates. Found in Golden Age literature, colonial legal codes, and 19th-century medical texts. Carries heavy honor-economy weight: defloration without marriage constituted 'deshonra.'

definition: From Hymen, Greek god of marriage; in Spanish literary usage, refers to the wedding, the marital union, and by extension the sexual consummation of marriage.
notes: Primarily a poetic synecdoche: the god's name stands for the rite and its consummation. Used by Lope de Vega, Góngora, and other Golden Age poets. In modern Spanish, 'himeneo' is essentially unrecognizable outside classical-education contexts; the anatomical cognate 'himen' (hymen) is far more current.

definition: Archaic Spanish term for the hymen or, by extension, the physical state of virginity; primarily an anatomical reference to the membranous structure at the vaginal opening.
notes: From Latin 'virgo' (virgin maiden). Used in older medical texts and Golden Age literature where the hymen was treated as proof of chastity. Modern speakers recognize 'virgo' chiefly as a zodiac sign; the anatomical meaning requires context. Current medical term is 'himen.'

definition: Archaic collective euphemism for women as a sex, emphasizing their beauty and erotic appeal; the Spanish equivalent of the English 'the fair sex.'
notes: Patronizing 18th–19th century idiom treating all women as a unified class defined by attractiveness and desirability. Appeared widely in Enlightenment-era Spanish literature, journalism, and conduct manuals. Now considered sexist and archaic; occasionally deployed ironically in modern usage.

definition: The marriage bed or bridal chamber; a poetic and literary metonym for the conjugal bed where a married couple consummmates their union.
notes: From Greek 'thalamos' (inner chamber). Common in Golden Age poetry and drama as a metonym for marital sexual union. In modern Spanish, 'tálamo' primarily denotes the neurological thalamus (part of the brain); the nuptial meaning is effectively dead outside literary contexts.

definition: Concupiscence; in Catholic theology, the inherited disordered inclination of human nature toward sin, especially the irrational drive toward sensual and sexual pleasure.
notes: Key term in Augustinian and Thomistic moral theology; the Spanish form mirrors the Latin exactly. Recognition is concentrated among those with formal religious or theological education; general-population recognition has declined with secularization.

definition: Intense sexual desire or libido; a Latinate literary term for lustful appetite, closely related to 'lujuria' but with a more visceral, sensory connotation.
notes: Directly from Latin 'libido.' Less common than 'lujuria' in Spanish; restricted to highly literary or scholarly registers. Some speakers conflate it with 'líbido' (the psychoanalytic term). Stress falls on the second syllable: li-BÍ-di-ne. Very low modern recognition outside classical literature contexts.

definition: To lust; to act on or be consumed by carnal desire; the verbal form of 'lujuria,' meaning to engage in or be driven by lustful behavior.
notes: Rarely encountered in modern Spanish; 'lujurioso/a' (adjective) and 'lujuria' (noun) survive in active use while the verb has retreated almost entirely to archaic literary texts. Conjugates as a regular -ar verb but practically unused in speech or contemporary writing.

definition: Literally 'weak flesh'; a religious idiom for the human body's inherent vulnerability to sexual temptation, drawn from Catholic doctrine on the frailty of physical human nature.
english_term: the weakness of the flesh, the flesh is weak
notes: Derives from the biblical phrase 'el espíritu está dispuesto, pero la carne es débil' (Matthew 26:41, Vulgate: 'caro autem infirma'). Used rhetorically to excuse or contextualize sexual sin by attributing it to bodily frailty rather than willful vice. Still widely understood in Catholic-formation cultures; occasionally ironic in modern usage.

definition: Historical Spanish legal term for statutory rape or the coercive or deceptive defloration of a minor or virgin; distinct from forcible rape ('violación'), covering seduction-based first sexual contact without constituting forcible assault.
notes: Persists in several Latin American criminal codes as a specific charge between seduction and forcible rape; in modern Spain largely subsumed by broader sexual offense statutes.

definition: Archaic medical term for sexually transmitted infections, derived from Venus, goddess of love; the dominant clinical phrase until replaced by 'enfermedad de transmisión sexual (ETS)' and later 'infección de transmisión sexual (ITS)' in the 1990s–2000s.
notes: Direct cognate of English 'venereal disease'; both fell from clinical use simultaneously across Western medical communities; still understood but marked as dated.

definition: More archaic variant of 'enfermedad venérea,' literally 'venereal evil' or 'venereal sickness'; encountered primarily in 19th- and early 20th-century Spanish medical writing and literature.
notes: Even more dated than 'enfermedad venérea'; the noun 'mal' (evil/illness) marks it as pre-modern medical register; rarely encountered outside historical texts.

definition: Archaic Greco-Latin term for a woman who has sex with other women, particularly through genital rubbing; the historical medical and moralizing label for what is now called a lesbian.
notes: Derived from Greek 'tribein' (to rub); used in Inquisition-era and early modern medical texts; almost entirely replaced by 'lesbiana' in contemporary usage; occasionally reclaimed in academic or queer historical contexts.

definition: Archaic literary and early sexological term for female homosexuality or lesbianism, named after the Greek lyric poet Sappho of Lesbos; used predominantly in 19th- and early 20th-century Spanish letters and sexology.
notes: Near-perfect cognate of English 'sapphism'; found in modernista and Generation of '98 literary criticism; virtually absent from contemporary Spanish except in historical analysis.

definition: Adjective meaning 'sapphic': relating to female homosexuality or to the poetic style of Sappho; used in literary and archaic contexts to describe love between women.
notes: Seeing selective revival in contemporary LGBTQ+ literary and academic spaces as a gentler or more aestheticized alternative to 'lesbiana'; still predominantly archaic in everyday register.

definition: Historical Spanish term for a licensed or municipally tolerated brothel, especially the institutionalized sex establishments of medieval and Golden Age Spain; etymologically related to 'mancebo' (young man).
notes: Refers specifically to the regulated prostitution system of early modern Spain; carries significant historiographical weight in scholarship on gender and sexuality in the Siglo de Oro; not a direct synonym for modern 'burdel'.

definition: Literally 'female' (the biological/zoological term); when applied to human women it is either archaic/crude objectification reducing a woman to her sex, or in contemporary reggaeton and urban slang, an admiring term for an attractive woman.

definition: Spanish internet slang (from English 'pack') for a collection or archive of someone's explicit or nude photos and videos, typically compiled and circulated without the subject's consent.

definition: Spanish internet phrasal verb meaning 'to ask someone for their pack': to request that another person send their nude or explicit photos, typically unsolicited and frequently directed at minors or strangers online.
notes: The predatory and minor-targeting dimension is statistically frequent; constitutes grooming when directed at minors; widely discussed in Spanish digital safety campaigns aimed at teenagers.

definition: Spanish internet phrase meaning 'to make or compile a pack': to gather someone's explicit images from multiple sources and aggregate them into a collection, typically for distribution without the subject's consent.

definition: Spanish verb derived from English 'to leak': to non-consensually distribute someone's private or explicit images or videos online; to publish intimate content without the subject's consent.

notes: Used in Spanish primarily in its English form; concentration among younger bilingual urban speakers and influencer culture; 'trampa del deseo' exists as a calque but is rarely used.

definition: English acronym 'Friends With Benefits' used directly in Spanish dating and internet discourse: a sexual arrangement between friends with no romantic commitment or exclusivity.
notes: Recognition concentrated among younger Spanish speakers with Anglophone internet exposure; native equivalents 'amigos con derechos' (Mexico/LA) or 'amigos con beneficios' exist and are more common in spoken Spanish.

definition: Loanword from English: a casual sexual encounter between people with no expectation of an ongoing relationship; also refers broadly to the dating-app culture enabling such encounters.
notes: Fully integrated into Spanish-language dating app culture and youth vernacular; also used as a verb 'hookupear' or 'hacer un hookup' in some communities; Grindr and Tinder have accelerated adoption.

definition: Spanish adaptation of 'alpha male': in manosphere discourse, a dominant, confident, sexually successful man who commands high social status and attracts women without visible effort; valorized earnestly within the subculture and mocked outside it.
notes: Direct calque of 'alpha male'; used both earnestly by manosphere adherents and ironically by critics; widely disseminated across Spanish-speaking regions via YouTube, TikTok, and podcasts centered on 'masculinidad' discourse.

definition: English acronym 'Not Safe For Work' used directly in Spanish-language internet spaces as a content warning for sexually explicit, violent, or otherwise inappropriate material.
notes: Used without translation across Spanish-speaking internet communities; understood primarily by internet-literate users; the native paraphrase 'no apto para el trabajo' or 'no apto para menores' exists but NSFW dominates in digital contexts.

definition: Euphemism for sexually explicit material — pornography, nude images, or graphic sexual content — widely used on digital platforms, in legal frameworks, app store ratings, and content warnings as a platform-safe alternative to 'pornografía'.
notes: The standard compliance-friendly euphemism across Spanish-language digital spaces; appears in platform terms of service, parental guidance labels, and child-protection legislation; directly mirrors English 'explicit content' as a regulatory category.

definition: Phrase meaning 'for adults only,' used as a content warning for sexually explicit or age-restricted material online and in broadcast media.
notes: Standard Spanish equivalent of NSFW or the 18+ label; used on websites, apps, and television alike. Non-transgressive in tone; purely regulatory.

definition: Sexual activity conducted via internet-based channels — live video calls, text chat, or audio — where participants engage sexually in real time without physical contact.

Broader than post_rejection_orbiting: stalkear can precede any romantic contact and implies active surveillance rather than passive engagement after rejection. Well-understood across all age-connected demographics.

notes: Used without phonological or morphological adaptation across all Spanish-speaking regions. Recognized even by speakers who do not use it actively.

definition: A mutual match on a dating app — primarily Tinder — where both parties signal explicitly sexual rather than romantic intent; also the person so matched.

'Titillation,' 'prurience,' and 'forbidden desire' each cover partial aspects but miss the keynote of pleasurable wrongness.
